clauses.why: An initial-off state exists only because the spec adds an enable/disable switch; a builder could ship the bot usable on install.
Withholding already-pending replies when authorization changes mid-flight requires re-checking access at delivery; nothing in a basic bot needs it.
Server-side idempotency against replayed or duplicated send actions, surviving refresh, is real work a working dev-org bot does not need.
A pre-submission disclosure notice about xAI processing is not required for a development-org Grok bot to work or be used safely.
States a provider-side retention fact; it gives the builder nothing to build or configure.
A rejected save leaving the prior value in place is generic platform behaviour true of any Salesforce configuration.
Coherence guarantees for configuration changes overlapping in-flight submissions are concurrency engineering a simple dev-org bot does not require.
Forbids a resend-on-config-change behaviour no builder would add; already implied by zero automatic retries, so it decides nothing.
A separate enable/disable kill switch is beyond the request; access can already be stopped by removing grants or the bot.
Withholding pending replies on disablement depends on the spec-introduced kill switch and requires delivery-time state checks.
Re-enablement exists only because of the spec-introduced enable/disable control.
A consolidated setup-status view including enablement state goes beyond what is needed to build and use the bot.
A fine-grained administrator diagnostic taxonomy across fifteen failure kinds is beyond a working bot; generic failure reporting would suffice.
Restates a 100-callout governor a one-callout-per-attempt bot never reaches; it requires nothing beyond showing failure, already covered.
Restates the 120-second cumulative callout governor, which the 45-second deadline already precludes; nothing actionable for the builder.
Describes a Developer Edition concurrency limit and that attempts may fail; it asks the builder to do nothing specific.
Restates the callout message-size governor; a 4,000-code-point prompt never approaches it, so it decides nothing.
Salesforce Apex heap limits are 6 MB synchronous and 12 MB asynchronous, not 10 MB and 25 MB.
Restates the CPU governor without any builder action beyond not reporting success, which is already covered.
Restates the long-running request governor, which excludes callout wait; it gives the builder nothing to act on.
Restates the uncommitted-work callout rule for a bot that performs no DML; it decides nothing for the builder.
Restates the daily async Apex quota conditionally on an unchosen route; no actionable requirement follows.
Release rollback to a prior bot version is release management the request for creating a dev-org bot does not call for.
A verified first-release undo procedure is a duty beyond creating the bot in a development org.
Rollback scoping exists only because the spec introduces rollback capability.
Rollback-with-inference-disabled combines two spec-introduced features, rollback and the kill switch.
Behaviour of pending interactions across release changes arises only from spec-introduced rollback and release management.
States scratch-org lifespan facts; nothing for a builder to implement.
States Developer Edition inactivity deletion policy with unconfirmed details; nothing for a builder to implement.
Disaster-recovery reinstallation into a replacement org is an operational duty beyond creating the bot once.
Production deployment test gates concern a future promotion the spec itself places out of scope.
Production Apex coverage requirements apply only to a future promotion beyond the requested development org.
States that unit tests mock callouts; it restates C-77's live-verification requirement and adds nothing actionable.
Credential provisioning in future destination orgs concerns packaging and promotion beyond the requested development org.
AppExchange security review concerns a public listing the request never asks for.
